definition: A mediator is a neutral third party who helps two sides in a dispute reach their own agreement.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mediator. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mediator should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The strike ended only after a federal mediator got the airline and the union back to the same table.
A go-between is weaker than a mediator: carrying messages across the divide is the whole job, while a mediator actively works the two sides toward a settlement.
An arbitrator goes further than a mediator — a mediator guides the talks but decides nothing, while an arbitrator hears both sides and hands down a ruling that binds them.
A go-between carries messages across a divide and stops there. A mediator does more than ferry words — a mediator steers the two sides toward a settlement they write themselves.

A peacemaker is anyone who tries to end a quarrel, by any means and from any position — even from inside the fight. A mediator works from a precise spot: outside the dispute, neutral, and welcome to both sides.

A mediator is a neutral third party who helps two sides in a dispute reach their own agreement.
Neither brother would speak to the other about their late father's hardware store, so the family hired a mediator.
She had no power to award the store to anyone — but by the second session she had each brother pricing the other's plan, and by Friday they had drawn up a buyout both could sign.
A mediator stands in the middle of a dispute and belongs to neither side.
The word insists on two limits: neutrality — a mediator argues for no one — and restraint — unlike a judge or an arbitrator, a mediator decides nothing.
The parties keep the power; the mediator keeps them talking.
neutral / procedural — courtrooms, contracts, diplomacy
Mediator is the word courts, unions, and diplomats use for the neutral in the middle — precise about both neutrality and limits.
If the third party rules, say arbitrator or judge; if they argue one side, say advocate.
And keep the sound-alike straight: mediation settles disputes; meditation is what you do on a quiet cushion.

The longest feud at Maplewood Middle School was not between students but between the band and the drama club, who shared one stage and agreed on nothing.
The principal declined to impose a schedule.
Instead she brought in a mediator: a retired teacher with no ties to either group, acceptable to both.
He set the ground rules, kept each meeting from collapsing, and asked the questions no one else would ask.
What he never did was decide.
When the clubs finally produced a calendar, every line of it was their own.
The drama teacher framed the last page; the band director keeps a copy in the tuba locker.
